title: Gaussian Boson Sampling for Asset Clustering in Statistical Arbitrage Portfolios
authors: Dayne Marcus Lopena, Daniel Buguks, Zhenghao Li, Ewan Mer, Shana H. Winston, Shang Yu, Mihai Cucuringu, Del Rajan, Philip Intallura, Raj B. Patel
abstract: Gaussian Boson Sampling (GBS) provides a native photonic quantum heuristic for sampling dense subgraphs from adjacency matrices, offering a scalable physical approach to combinatorial graph search problems. Simultaneously, correlation matrix clustering algorithms, such as Spectral and SPONGE, have established robust benchmarks for identifying co-moving assets from correlation matrices in statistical arbitrage (StatArb) strategies. In this work, we map S&P 500 residual correlation data into GBS-compatible adjacency matrices. We benchmark those classical clustering algorithms against two quantum clustering algorithms, GBS Boost and our novel GBS Roots, to construct dynamic, market-neutral portfolios over a rolling one-year window. Simulations across distinct macroeconomic regimes reveal that quantum clustering generates superior alpha within large stock universes during periods of high volatility, effectively isolating structural market idiosyncrasies. Crucially, this economic advantage persists under simulated low-loss conditions and extends into high-loss regimes via the application of coherent displacement to compensate for photon loss. Our findings underscore the efficacy of GBS-derived graph clustering in constructing robust StatArb portfolios, establishing a quantum foundation for broader quantitative finance applications.
summary: This work pioneers the use of Gaussian Boson Sampling (GBS) to cluster assets within financial portfolios for statistical arbitrage. By mapping correlation matrices into photonic graph structures, the authors propose quantum algorithms that outperform classical methods during volatile market conditions. It establishes a novel quantum heuristic framework linking quantum optics to quantitative finance.
main_problem: The paper applies Gaussian Boson Sampling (GBS) to solve the Max-Agree Correlation Clustering Problem (MACCP) for constructing robust Statistical Arbitrage (StatArb) portfolios.
main_result: Quantum clustering methods using GBS generate superior alpha during high volatility periods compared to classical algorithms, establishing a quantum foundation for quantitative finance applications.
method: The authors map asset correlation data into adjacency matrices and use specialized quantum algorithms (GBS Boost, GBS Roots) that leverage GBS sampling to iteratively find optimal dense subgraphs representing co-moving assets.
model_or_system: The physical model is based on Gaussian Boson Sampling using squeezed vacuum states interfering in a linear interferometer. The process simulates the measurement of photon statistics proportional to the hafnian of the correlation submatrix.
key_observables: Alpha generation, Sharpe Ratio (ShR), Sortino Ratio (SoR), Weighted Density (WD), and Jaccard similarity across rolling time windows.
important_parameters: Universe size ($N$), photon loss factor ($\eta$), required sample budget $H = O(N \log N)$, and the correlation matrix derived from S&P 500 residuals.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that maximizing intra-cluster correlations (MACCP) directly translates to profitable arbitrage signals. Furthermore, quantum advantage demonstrations are heuristic, not complexity-theoretic proofs.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the GBS-driven StatArb framework, showing data processing, iterative clustering procedures (GBS Roots), and performance comparisons across varying stock universes ($N$).
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem by linking graph clustering to StatArb. It details mapping correlation matrices to GBS inputs, presents quantum algorithms like GBS Roots for MACCP, benchmarks these against classical methods using financial metrics, and analyzes scaling limits.
why_interesting: While applied to finance, the core mechanism involves simulating complex many-body interactions (photon interference) via GBS to solve a combinatorial optimization problem (graph clustering), which is relevant to understanding resource limitations in quantum simulation for structured data analysis.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

Zeroing the main diagonal yields the adjacency matrix of the correlation graph. (b) The GBS clustering procedure. The correlation graph is encoded into a GBS device through its adjacency matrix. The device generates subgraph samples, which are evaluated against an edge-weight criterion to select the highest-scoring cluster. This selected subgraph is then removed from the graph to produce a residual graph, and the process is iteratively applied to generate a complete partition of the correlation network.
